title: COLD OPEN
text: January fifteenth, nineteen nineteen. Boston, Massachusetts. An unusually warm afternoon in the North End. Children are walking home from school. Workers are on their lunch break. And above them, on a hill by the harbor, stands a steel tank holding two point three million gallons of molasses. It has been groaning for years. Today, it will not hold.

title: THE TANK
text: The tank belonged to the Purity Distilling Company, and it stood at five twenty-nine Commercial Street. Fifty feet tall. Ninety feet wide. Built in nineteen fifteen to store molasses brought in by ship. Why? Because molasses can be turned into industrial alcohol, and alcohol was also a key ingredient in munitions.

title: WARNING SIGNS
text: There was a reason for the hurry. The next day, January sixteenth, the Eighteenth Amendment would be ratified. Prohibition was coming. The company wanted to make as much alcohol as it could. The tank was built fast, and it was barely tested. The treasurer who oversaw it, Arthur Jell, had no engineering training. He never even filled it with water to check for leaks. When the tank was finally filled with molasses, it leaked so badly that the company simply painted it brown, to hide the stains. Neighbors came with buckets to collect the sweet drips. Every time it was filled, the walls groaned. Nobody listened.

title: THE DAY
text: On January fourteenth, a ship delivered a fresh load of warm molasses. And the weather changed. In just two days, the temperature in Boston had jumped from about two degrees to over forty. At about twelve thirty on the fifteenth, the tank gave way. Witnesses felt the ground shake. They heard a roar, like an elevated train. Some said it sounded like a machine gun. That was the sound of the rivets, shooting out of the steel.

title: THE WAVE
text: Two point three million gallons, about thirteen thousand tons, poured out all at once. A wave of molasses, up to twenty-five feet high at its peak, raced down Commercial Street at around thirty-five miles per hour. It was forty percent heavier than water. It tipped a streetcar off its tracks. It slammed steel panels from the tank into the elevated railway, and bent the girders. It lifted a truck and threw it into the harbor. Buildings were torn from their foundations, and crushed.

title: TRAPPED
text: Then, the molasses did something water never does. It cooled, and it thickened. Scientists call it a non-Newtonian fluid. Under pressure, it flows fast. Once it settles, it turns thick, and it holds on. The Boston Post wrote that horses died like flies on flypaper. The more they struggled, the deeper they sank. People were caught the same way. A boy named Anthony di Stasio was carried on the crest of the wave, then rolled like a pebble. He heard his mother call his name. He could not answer, because his throat was packed with molasses.

title: RESCUE
text: The first to arrive were one hundred and sixteen cadets from the training ship Nantucket, docked nearby. They ran several blocks, and waded into the knee-deep syrup to pull out survivors. Police, soldiers, sailors and Red Cross nurses followed. Some nurses dove right into the molasses. Doctors set up a hospital in a nearby building. Rescuers searched for four days. Some victims were so coated that they could not be recognized. Others were swept into the harbor, and were found three or four months later.

title: THE COUNT
text: Twenty-one people died that day. Not from water. Not from fire. From molasses. About one hundred and fifty more were injured. Cleanup crews used salt water from fireboats to wash the streets, and sand to soak up the rest. The harbor stayed brown until summer. Molasses was carried by shoes onto trains, into homes, onto telephones. It was said that everything a Bostonian touched was sticky.

title: THE TRIAL
text: Then came the question: who was to blame? The company, now owned by United States Industrial Alcohol, said anarchists had blown up the tank. One hundred and nineteen residents sued. It was one of the first class-action lawsuits in Massachusetts. After three years of hearings, the court-appointed auditor, Hugh Ogden, ruled that the company was responsible. It paid six hundred and twenty-eight thousand dollars. The families of the dead reportedly received about seven thousand dollars each.

title: THE CAUSE
text: Later studies found the truth. In twenty fourteen, engineers found that the steel was only half as thick as it should have been, and that it was brittle. Cracks had started at the rivets. In twenty sixteen, researchers at Harvard tested a scale model with cold corn syrup. Their conclusion: yes, the wave really was that fast. And yes, it really did thicken quickly enough to trap people before they could be freed.

title: LEGACY
text: The company never rebuilt the tank. Today, a baseball field and a playground stand on the spot, and a small plaque at the park remembers what happened. For decades, people said that on warm summer days, the North End still smelled of molasses. The disaster changed the law. After it, buildings needed to be approved by a licensed architect and engineer. On the hundredth anniversary, people stood in a circle on the field, marking the edge of the tank, and read aloud the names of all twenty-one victims.

title: OUTRO
text: A tank. A warm day. A warning that nobody wanted to hear. This is the story they don’t teach you in school.
